one_liner: Zig-vs-C++-vs-Go benchmark repo: Zig ReleaseFast wasm32-wasi edges Emscripten -O2 C++ on one integer matmul loop.
what_it_does: A benchmark playground, not a library: three equivalent single-file programs (benchmark.zig, benchmark.cpp, benchmark.go) run 10,000 chained rounds of a 64x64 u64 matrix multiply followed by an FNV-1a hash of the product, then print the final hash, elapsed time and ops/sec. A Makefile builds each program natively and to WebAssembly (zig -target wasm32-wasi, em++ to a standalone .wasm, GOOS=wasip1) and runs it pinned to CPU 0 with taskset under Wasmer (Cranelift and LLVM), Wasmtime and WasmEdge. There is no API; the 'contender' is the Zig compiler's wasm32-wasi output, which you adopt by writing the module in Zig.
how_it_is_fast: No special technique: all three sources are the same naive i-j-k triple loop over stack arrays with wrapping 64-bit multiplies. The Zig build is ReleaseFast (LLVM at full optimisation, safety checks off) while the Emscripten build is -O2, and neither enables wasm SIMD (no -msimd128, no simd128 CPU feature), so both emit scalar i64 code and the 1.29x gap more plausibly reflects the optimisation level than the language. Zig wasm under WasmEdge's LLVM-based JIT (15,305 ops/sec) lands on Zig native ReleaseFast (15,386), so for this scalar loop the runtime recovers native code quality.
when_to_use: As a template for comparing standalone WASI runtimes on a scalar 64-bit integer kernel: make bench-wasm-runtimes loops the Go, C++ and Zig modules over Wasmer Cranelift, Wasmer LLVM, Wasmtime and WasmEdge JIT.
To sanity-check that Zig's wasm32-wasi output keeps up with Emscripten's for a CPU-bound, non-SIMD integer loop running outside a browser (WASI command modules).
When choosing between Zig and Go for WASI modules: Go's wasip1 build ran 3,230 vs Zig's 15,305 ops/sec on WasmEdge (4.7x, derived from page data).
To see how much the runtime matters: the same C++ module ran 11,855 ops/sec on WasmEdge and 6,911 on Wasmer Cranelift (1.7x, derived from page data).
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Zig beats C++ for wasm: the baseline is em++ -O2 rather than -O3, and the Zig wasm row exists only for WasmEdge; rebuild the C++ module at -O3 before concluding anything.
For browser, Node.js or V8 workloads: nothing runs in a JavaScript engine and there are no JavaScript or TypeScript rows.
For SIMD-heavy or floating-point kernels: neither wasm build enables simd128, and the only workload is a 64x64 u64 matmul plus FNV-1a hash.
As reusable code: there is no library, no tests and no CI; 0 stars, 8 commits all made on 2025-09-01.
For statistically sound numbers: each README row is one process run with one wall-clock timing, no repeat count, no variance and unstated compiler and runtime versions.

integration.form: source-drop (three standalone benchmark programs and a Makefile; not a library)
integration.dependencies: Zig 0.13+, Emscripten (emsdk 'latest', unpinned), Go 1.24+, g++ or clang++, taskset, and the Wasmer, Wasmtime and WasmEdge CLIs
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.13+ and Go 1.24+ per the README; C++20; Emscripten version not stated
integration.platforms: Linux host for the Makefile (taskset, ~/.wasmedge/bin path); the wasm32-wasi modules run on any WASI runtime

gotchas: Stack-size asymmetry (possible harness flaw, not reproduced here because nothing was built): matmul_and_hash keeps three 64x64 u64 arrays on the stack, about 96 KB per call. Zig 0.13 gives wasm32-wasi executables a 16 MiB stack by default (src/link/Wasm.zig), but Emscripten's default STACK_SIZE is 64 KB and overflow is unchecked at -O2 (settings.js: 'it will fail silently'); the em++ line sets no -sSTACK_SIZE. A rebuild of the C++ wasm module may therefore trap or corrupt memory, and the README omits the printed Result hashes that would show all builds computed the same value.

The per-language targets (make bench-cpp-wasm, bench-zig-wasm, bench-go-wasm) run under Wasmer's default engine; the WasmEdge rows come from make bench-wasm-runtimes, which also runs the Zig module on Wasmer Cranelift, Wasmer LLVM and Wasmtime, yet the README publishes no Zig numbers for those three runtimes.

The README note that Zig WASM is 'nearly matching C++ optimized native' contradicts its own table (15,305 vs 49,279 ops/sec, 3.2x slower). The 4.2x 'C++ optimized' native gain mixes -O2 to -O3, LTO and -march=native on a Zen 5 CPU with AVX-512; GCC's -O3 loop interchange plus 64-bit vector multiplies is a likely cause (not measured), so it says nothing about wasm.
Makefile has dead targets: bench-cpp-wasm-opt depends on an undefined build-cpp-wasm-opt and runs a bench-cpp-opt.wasm nothing builds, and the help text lists a bench-wasm target that does not exist.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Unlike wasm-perf, Speedy.js or the Chankse JavaScript-vs-WebAssembly matmul study, which measure wasm against JavaScript in V8, this repo compares source languages (Zig, C++, Go) on standalone WASI runtimes, so it only fits a server-side WASI runtime or language question; for C++-to-wasm compiler quality, Cheerp's claim against Emscripten is the closer catalogued comparison, and neither is strong evidence.
verified_claims_summary: On one pinned core of an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (Ubuntu 24.04), the Zig ReleaseFast wasm32-wasi build ran 15,305 ops/sec under WasmEdge JIT against 11,855 for the same 64x64 u64 matmul + FNV-1a loop compiled by em++ -O2, about 1.29x (derived from page data). Each figure is a single run with unstated compiler and runtime versions, and native GCC -O3 -march=native C++ (49,279 ops/sec) beats both wasm builds by more than 3x.
status_note: Stale since 2025-09-01 (8 commits in one day, 0 stars, no issues), MIT-licensed and trivially copyable, but it is a benchmark playground rather than a component, and the -O2 vs ReleaseFast baseline plus a probable 64 KB Emscripten stack overflow in the C++ wasm build (not reproduced) mean the 1.29x should not be relied on.
